strengths: Genuine and novel theoretical contribution: the paper proposes the first Neyman-orthogonal learning objective for ranking treatment effects, and Theorem 5.1 (with the full derivation in Appendix C) rigorously verifies orthogonality with respect to all three nuisance components (mu1, mu0, e) using the correct zero-mean properties of the doubly robust score and the inverse-propensity terms.

Elegant technical construction: because binary cross-entropy is affine in its label, the influence-function correction can be absorbed directly into the pseudo-labels (Eq. 12), so the second stage reduces to standard pairwise BCE ranking. This keeps the implementation simple and model-agnostic while embedding orthogonality entirely in label construction.

Clear characterization of population optima (Theorem 5.2 and Appendix D): the paper shows the orthogonal loss shares the soft loss's minimizers g(x)=(1/kappa)tau(x)+c and provides a thoughtful discussion of the kappa-induced bias-variance tradeoff (flatness of the loss as kappa->0 versus amplified pseudo-label variance).

Good positioning relative to prior work (Table 1) and a practically relevant problem setting (healthcare triage, targeted marketing, policy targeting); the distinction from policy learning in Appendix A is well argued (threshold-independent global ordering).

Consistent direction of empirical results: Rank-Learner has the highest mean AUTOC/policy value against T-learner, DR-learner, and plug-in ranker in essentially all reported settings, with the largest and clearest gains in low-data regimes (e.g., n=250: 1.28 +/- 0.03 vs DR-learner 1.16 +/- 0.12), and pair subsampling is shown to be an effective scaling strategy.
weaknesses: Presentation flaw: the manuscript contains two separate sections both titled 'Introduction' (Sections 1 and 2), an obvious preparation error that signals a lack of care and disrupts the structure of the paper.

Empirical gains are marginal and frequently within noise. In Table 4 (MOVIELENS) Rank-Learner is 1.35 +/- 0.01 vs DR-learner 1.34 +/- 0.02; in Table 3 for n>=500 the differences (e.g., 1.34 vs 1.33/1.32) are tiny relative to reported standard deviations. No statistical significance testing is performed despite five seeds, so the central 'consistently outperforms' claim is not strongly supported in the moderate/large-sample and semi-synthetic regimes.

The 'consistently outperforms' claim is contradicted by the model-specific baseline: in Table 7 the tree ranker of Kamran et al. (2024) attains higher AUTOC and policy value at n=100 (1.01 +/- 0.16 vs 0.94 +/- 0.21), which the paper itself acknowledges.

Tension with the central motivation: at any finite kappa the population minimizer is a scaled CATE (1/kappa)tau(x)+c, i.e., the loss still identifies tau up to scale rather than merely its ordering. The 'ranking is an easier problem' argument only holds in the kappa->0 limit, where pseudo-label variance is amplified. This somewhat undercuts the stated motivation that the method solves a strictly easier problem than CATE estimation.

Reproducibility concerns: the code repository link is truncated/broken in the manuscript, and the semi-synthetic data-generating processes are explicitly deferred to that repository rather than specified, making those experiments hard to reproduce. The synthetic DGP is described in detail, but the semi-synthetic ones are not.

The semi-synthetic benchmarks combine real covariates with fully simulated treatments and outcomes under the same design principles as the synthetic data, so the 'realistic' claim is limited; there is no evaluation with real treatment effects or outcomes.

The 'model-agnostic' property is claimed but only demonstrated with a single feedforward NN architecture (one hidden layer, ReLU); no alternative model classes (e.g., trees, linear models, boosting) are tested to substantiate the claim.

strengths: Proposes a novel orthogonal two-stage learner that combines pairwise ranking with influence-function-based Neyman-orthogonalization for treatment effect ranking.
Provides a formal orthogonality proof (Theorem 5.1) and characterizes population minimizers (Theorem 5.2) for the proposed loss.
The method is model-agnostic and includes a practical pair-subsampling strategy to scale pairwise training.
Reports experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks across sample sizes and overlap levels, with some observed improvements over baselines.
Discusses limitations such as the bias-variance tradeoff in the smoothness parameter κ and sensitivity to limited overlap.
weaknesses: Experimental comparison is confounded: Rank-Learner and the plug-in ranker are tuned using the approximated AUTOC (the evaluation metric), while the T- and DR-learner CATE baselines are tuned using standard CATE validation loss. This biases results in favor of the proposed method and undermines the central claim of outperforming standard CATE estimators.

Evaluation does not directly measure ranking quality (e.g., Spearman or Kendall rank correlation); it reports only AUTOC and mean policy value, which are policy-value metrics and do not fully assess correctness of the global treatment effect ordering.
Empirical gains are marginal: in many settings the differences from the DR-learner are within one standard deviation or only 0.01–0.03 AUTOC, and no statistical significance tests are provided.

Reproducibility is limited: the semi-synthetic data-generating processes are not fully specified in equations, the code repository is referenced without a link, and key details (e.g., exact AUTOC approximation, clipping frequency, pair sampling) are missing.

Theoretical claims are overstated: the paper advertises 'strong theoretical guarantees,' but only local orthogonality is proved; no finite-sample convergence rates, regret bounds, or sample-complexity comparisons are given for the ranking task.

The motivation that the method avoids solving the harder CATE estimation problem is only valid in the limit κ→0; for any fixed finite κ, the population optimum is a scaled CATE up to a constant, so the method still imposes magnitude constraints and estimates treatment effects up to scale.

The orthogonal pseudo labels can fall outside [0,1], and the paper clips them as a 'simple stabilization strategy' without analyzing how often clipping occurs or whether it breaks the claimed orthogonality in finite samples.

Presentation is poor: the manuscript contains two separate 'Introduction' sections (Sections 1 and 2), Table 2 is garbled, several reference years are inconsistent (e.g., Burges and Shaked 2005, Buyl et al. 2007, Cao et al. 2018), and there are notation typos (e.g., L^bix).
The improvement over the non-orthogonal plug-in ranker is also small, so the practical benefit of the orthogonal correction is not convincingly demonstrated in the tested regimes.

The main text compares only to T-learner, DR-learner, and a plug-in ranker; the tree-based direct ranking baseline appears only in the appendix, and other modern CATE or ranking baselines are not considered.

strengths: Introduces the first Neyman-orthogonal two-stage learner for directly ranking treatment effects, combining influence-function-based orthogonalization with a pairwise ranking loss.

Provides a rigorous derivation of the efficient influence function and proves Neyman-orthogonality of the proposed loss with respect to all nuisance components (Theorem 5.1), as well as characterizing its population minimizers (Theorem 5.2).
The method is model-agnostic and can be instantiated with arbitrary machine learning models; practical strategies such as pair subsampling and tuning κ via AUTOC make it scalable.

Experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks show consistent improvements over standard CATE estimators (T- and DR-learners) and a non-orthogonal plug-in ranker, with the largest gains in small-sample and limited-overlap regimes where nuisance error is most pronounced.
Clear positioning relative to related work, transparent discussion of identification assumptions, and an appropriate impact statement acknowledging responsible use.
weaknesses: The central motivation that CATE learning solves a harder problem than necessary is overstated: the proposed orthogonal loss still has population minimizer g(x)=τ(x)/κ+c, which requires recovering the scaled shape of the CATE up to an additive constant, not just the ordering. The truly easier binary ranking loss is not orthogonalized directly; the relaxation relative to full CATE estimation is only scale and shift.

The paper claims 'strong theoretical guarantees' but only proves orthogonality and characterizes population minimizers; it does not provide finite-sample convergence rates or ranking regret bounds that would justify robustness of the learned ranking function in finite samples.

Empirical improvements over the orthogonal DR-learner are modest and sometimes within one standard deviation (e.g., MovieLens: 1.35±0.01 vs 1.34±0.02). At the smallest sample size (n=100), the tree ranker of Kamran et al. (2024) outperforms Rank-Learner. Baselines are limited to simple feedforward neural networks; no comparison to state-of-the-art CATE estimators such as causal forests or gradient boosting is provided.

Reproducibility is partially limited: the semi-synthetic data-generating processes are not fully specified in the manuscript but only referenced to an accompanying code repository, and the link is missing in the submitted version. The clipping of pseudo labels to (0,1) is used as a practical stabilizer but lacks theoretical justification.

Presentation issues: duplicate 'Introduction' headings (Sections 1 and 2), an incomplete Table 2 missing entries for the orthogonal loss row, inconsistent notation (t vs \hat{t} vs \tilde{t}), reference year errors (e.g., Buyl et al. 2007 vs 2023; Chernozhukov et al. 2021 vs 2018), and a typo 'L^{bix}' in Appendix D.2.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically relevant problem: directly learning a ranking of treatment effects from observational data, rather than estimating CATE magnitudes and ranking post hoc. The framing (ranking only requires order preservation, so full CATE recovery is unnecessarily hard) is clear and well motivated.

The core methodological contribution is novel and principled. The authors construct a smooth pairwise (soft) ranking loss and then apply a standard influence-function-based one-step correction to obtain an orthogonal objective. The construction is technically correct: I verified that absorbing the correction into the pseudo-labels is valid because binary cross-entropy is affine in its label (Eq. 56), so the orthogonal loss equals the plug-in loss plus the one-step correction.

The theory is presented with full derivations. The Neyman-orthogonality proof (Appendix C.4) correctly exploits the zero conditional mean of the doubly robust score and of the treatment-indicator weights for each nuisance component (mu1, mu0, e), and Theorem 5.2 correctly characterizes the population minimizer as g(x) = tau(x)/kappa + c by evaluating the conditional expectation of the pseudo-label.

The experiments are broad and cover complementary regimes: a controlled synthetic benchmark with varying sample size, three semi-synthetic benchmarks with real covariates (MovieLens, MIMIC-III, CPS), and the real-world Criteo uplift benchmark with confounded training and randomized test data. Ablations on overlap, nuisance misspecification, kappa sensitivity, label clipping, and pair-subsampling strategies strengthen the empirical study.

The method is model-agnostic and the second stage reduces to standard pairwise ranking with modified labels, making it easy to implement with arbitrary ML models. The paper reports reproducibility-relevant details (architectures, hyperparameter grid, cross-fitting, AUTOC-based model selection) and indicates a code release.

The discussion of the smoothness parameter kappa (its bias-variance role, the population-optimum scaling, and the curvature argument in Appendix D.2) is thoughtful and connects the objective to the pure binary ranking loss in the limit.
weaknesses: The empirical advantage over the most relevant baseline, the (also orthogonal) DR-learner, is marginal and frequently within noise. On the semi-synthetic benchmarks (Table 4/8), Rank-Learner is 1.35+/-0.01 vs 1.34+/-0.02 (MovieLens), 1.18+/-0.02 vs 1.17+/-0.02 (MIMIC-III), and 0.95+/-0.01 vs 0.92+/-0.02 (CPS); these are essentially ties given only five seeds. The clear wins occur mainly over the non-orthogonal plug-in ranker and in small-sample synthetic settings (n<=250). No paired significance tests are reported, so the repeated claim that Rank-Learner "consistently outperforms" standard CATE estimators is only weakly supported.

The theoretical claims are overstated relative to what is proven. The paper advertises "strong theoretical guarantees, including robustness to estimation errors" and invokes "fast convergence rates" (Foster & Syrgkanis, 2023; Nie & Wager, 2021), but only establishes orthogonality of the population loss and its minimizers. No convergence rate, regret bound, or finite-sample guarantee for the learned (infinite-dimensional) ranking function is provided, and the additional conditions under which orthogonality implies fast rates are not verified for this ranking setting.

The additional baseline comparison (Appendix F.4.1, Table 12) shows that a sophisticated CATE estimator (FlexTENet) is essentially tied with Rank-Learner at the largest sample size (1.358 vs 1.358). This suggests that the advantage of direct orthogonal ranking may be limited once nuisance estimation is accurate, which is not fully reconciled with the paper's narrative that CATE estimation is solving an unnecessarily harder problem.

The main experiments use deliberately small feedforward networks with minimal tuning, which is a reasonable design to isolate effects but limits external validity; the paper acknowledges the absolute performance differs when matched to CATENets-style architectures, complicating cross-experiment comparison.

The Criteo results (Table 5/9) rest on large standard deviations (e.g., 5.19+/-1.87 at 50k), so the reported improvement, while largest in mean, is noisy and would benefit from significance testing or more seeds.

Presentation issues: the manuscript contains two consecutive sections both titled "Introduction" (the first appears to duplicate the abstract/summary), and the semi-synthetic data-generating processes are only referenced to the code repository rather than fully specified, which slightly hinders independent reproduction.
The AUTOC metric is not normalized (acknowledged), which makes it hard for readers to judge the practical magnitude of the reported differences across settings.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: ranking individuals by treatment effects under resource constraints, with clear motivating examples in healthcare, marketing, and public policy.

Provides a novel orthogonal pairwise ranking objective derived via influence functions. The derivation of the pseudo-label correction in Appendix C is technically detailed, and Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 give a coherent story: the loss is Neyman-orthogonal w.r.t. the nuisance functions and its population minimizer preserves the CATE ordering.
The method is model-agnostic and can be instantiated with arbitrary ML models; inference only requires pointwise evaluation of the learned scoring function, which is practical.

Includes a useful set of experiments: synthetic, three semi-synthetic datasets, Criteo, plus additional ACIC/IHDP results and robustness checks (overlap sensitivity, nuisance misspecification, kappa sensitivity, pair subsampling, clipping diagnostic).
Writing is generally clear, the positioning table is helpful, and the limitations of kappa and the soft-to-binary ranking interpolation are discussed in Appendix D.2.
weaknesses: Theoretical guarantees are incomplete. The paper proves local Neyman-orthogonality of the ideal loss, but provides no convergence rates, excess-risk bounds, or assumptions on nuisance estimators. Since the target is an ordering, orthogonality of a soft loss does not by itself imply ranking recovery rates. Claims of 'strong theoretical guarantees' and 'fast convergence rates' are therefore unsupported.

The implemented objective is not the one for which orthogonality is proven. The orthogonal pseudo-labels can lie outside (0,1), making the unclipped binary cross-entropy loss unbounded below. All experiments therefore clip labels to (0,1), which breaks exact orthogonality. The paper only offers an empirical gradient-sensitivity diagnostic for the clipped loss and no theory for it. This is a significant gap between theory and practice.

The framing 'without explicit CATE estimation' and 'directly targets ranking' is overstated. The pseudo-labels require an estimate of tau = mu1 - mu0, and for finite kappa the population optimum is g(x) = tau(x)/kappa + c, i.e. it still learns scaled CATE magnitudes. Only in the limit kappa -> 0 does the objective approach pure ranking, but kappa is finite and tuned in practice.

Empirical improvements are marginal and often within noise. For example, synthetic n=1000: Rank-Learner 1.34 vs DR-learner 1.33, T-learner 1.32, plug-in ranker 1.31; semi-synthetic MIMIC-III: 1.18 vs 1.17. Criteo differences have large standard deviations, and no significance tests are reported. In additional baselines, FlexTENet matches Rank-Learner at n=2000 (1.358 vs 1.358) and is competitive elsewhere, so the claim of 'consistently outperforms' is not strongly supported.

There is a likely tuning advantage for the ranking methods. Rank-Learner and the plug-in ranker tune kappa and other hyperparameters using an approximated AUTOC (a ranking metric), while the CATE baselines are selected using standard validation losses (e.g., MSE). This makes the comparison favorable to the proposed method and should be controlled (e.g., tune all methods for AUTOC or report both).

The benchmarks may be favorable to the method. In the synthetic and semi-synthetic DGPs, tau is a strictly increasing transformation of a latent score s(x), and treatment assignment depends on s(x); nuisance models can recover s(x), making ranking relatively easy. The real-world evaluation is limited to Criteo, and the tree ranker and other orthogonal ranking competitors are not evaluated on Criteo or semi-synthetic data.

Reproducibility is compromised: the code repository URL is missing/blank ('available at' with no link), and the semi-synthetic data-generating processes are only said to be in the code repository rather than fully specified in the paper. This makes independent reproduction difficult.

Presentation issues are serious for a main-track submission: the manuscript contains duplicate introductions ('1 Introduction' and '2 Introduction' with essentially identical text), Table 2 mislabels the soft loss as L^orth and has inconsistent notation, and there is no dedicated limitations section beyond a brief impact statement. Some references to 2026 venues also appear unverifiable.

The contribution is incremental: it combines existing orthogonal learning with pairwise ranking. While the derivation is nontrivial, there is no fundamentally new understanding of ranking or causal inference, and the empirical gains do not convincingly demonstrate practical superiority over well-tuned CATE estimators or strong CATE baselines.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: the paper proposes the first Neyman-orthogonal two-stage learner for directly ranking individuals by treatment effects, filling a clearly articulated gap (Table 1) between orthogonal CATE estimators and non-orthogonal/model-specific rankers.

The theory is sound and non-trivial. The influence-function-based derivation of the orthogonal ranking loss (Appendix C) is careful, and the cross-derivative checks of orthogonality with respect to mu_1, mu_0, and e (Theorem 5.1) appear correct. The population-minimizer characterization (Theorem 5.2, g(x) = tau(x)/kappa + c) is also derived correctly, and the neat observation that the affine BCE loss lets the correction be absorbed into the pseudo labels is elegant.

The method is genuinely model-agnostic and practical: orthogonality is injected only through the labels, leaving the second-stage problem as standard pairwise BCE; pair subsampling and clipping are sensible scaling/stabilization tricks, and the diagnostic in Fig. 7 supports that the (clipped) orthogonal objective is less sensitive to nuisance perturbations than the plug-in loss.

The empirical study is broad, covering a controlled synthetic DGP, three semi-synthetic datasets with realistic covariates, the real-world Criteo uplift benchmark, and additional ACIC/IHDP comparisons, plus ablations on overlap, nuisance misspecification, kappa sensitivity, pair subsampling, and label clipping.

Limitations of the approach (the kappa bias-variance trade-off, the divergence of the minimizer as kappa -> 0, and the effect of clipping on exact orthogonality) are discussed openly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The empirical gains are small and often within one standard deviation of the baselines. Against the DR-learner on the semi-synthetic benchmarks the differences are essentially ties (MovieLens 1.35+/-0.01 vs 1.34+/-0.02; MIMIC 1.18+/-0.02 vs 1.17+/-0.02; CPS 0.95+/-0.01 vs 0.92+/-0.02), and on the synthetic benchmark at n=2000 all methods converge to ~1.36-1.37. The claim that Rank-Learner 'consistently outperforms' is therefore overstated relative to the actual margins, and the Criteo improvements carry very large variance (e.g., 5.19+/-1.87 vs 4.44+/-1.12).

Despite the introduction's claim of 'strong theoretical guarantees,' only orthogonality and population-minimizer identification are proven. No finite-sample/convergence rate is provided, and orthogonality alone does not guarantee fast rates for the non-convex, pairwise loss actually optimized; the practical implications of the theory remain asserted rather than established.

There is a conceptual tension in the central motivation. At any finite kappa the population optimum is g(x) = (1/kappa)tau(x) + c, i.e., the full CATE shape up to an affine transform, so the 'ranking is an easier problem than CATE estimation' argument strictly holds only in the kappa -> 0 limit, where the minimizer is unbounded and (as the authors note) pseudo-label variance is amplified. It is not fully demonstrated that the method actually exploits the 'easier' structure in a way that explains its performance.

Presentation issues: the manuscript contains two sections both titled 'Introduction' (Sections 1 and 2) and duplicate section numbering (two sections numbered '2', the second being 'Related work'). This should be cleaned up.
Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of a code link: the text states the implementation 'is available at' with no URL, so the promised artifact cannot be located.

The most direct competitor, the tree ranker of Kamran et al. (2024), is relegated to Appendix F.4, where Rank-Learner only marginally edges it and FlexTENet (Table 12), weakening the strength of the head-to-head comparison against the closest prior work.
